揚琴以琴竹擊弦發聲，音色隨弦材與琴竹而變：銅弦較柔，鋼弦與銅纏低音弦較亮且音量較: The yangqin sounds when its bamboo beaters strike the strings, and the timbre changes with the string material and the beaters: bronze strings are softer, while steel strings and copper-wound bass strings are brighter and louder. One end of the beater is covered with rubber and gives a softer tone; the bare bamboo face strikes more sharply, and the tail of the beater can pluck the strings and make a glissando. A modern yangqin may have as many as five rows of bridges, arranged chromatically, and the 601 model has a range from the great octave to the four-line octave; a note is usually given one to five strings in a group to increase volume, the double-note beaters can strike several notes at once, and the bass notes ring on longer. Compared with the santur and the other dulcimers, the yangqin is struck with fingerless bamboo hammers on long wooden bridges, its notes ring longer, and the strings are usually damped with the palm.
揚琴可聽於江南絲竹、廣東音樂、潮州音樂、四川揚琴、東北揚琴、山東琴書、維吾爾木卡: The yangqin can be heard in Jiangnan sizhu, Cantonese music, Chaozhou music, Sichuan yangqin, Northeast yangqin, Shandong qinshu, Uyghur muqam and the Inner Mongolian errentai, and in Chinese orchestras it is scored as a plucked instrument, usually in the first row in front of the conductor, playing chords or arpeggios and accompanying solos for huqin, dizi and other instruments. For solo playing, Xiang Zuhua's 'Lin Chong's Night Flight' uses the double-note beaters; the Cantonese yangqin pieces edited by Yan Laolie — 'Han Tian Lei', 'Dao Chui Lian', 'Lian Huan Kou', 'Dao Chun Lai' and 'Gui Lai Yan' — mostly use the left-hand padding technique (zuoyin); and Liu Hanli's arrangements 'Panjigah Muqam Variations', 'Jinlingsi: Caprice of the Manchu Homeland' and 'Lishan Chiying' show its range and its handling of key changes.
揚琴屬擊弦樂器，源流未有定論，可能經陸路自伊朗桑圖爾或歐洲德西馬傳入，也可能經海: The yangqin is a struck string instrument, and its origins are not settled: it may have come overland from the Iranian santur or the European dulcimer, or by sea in Portuguese, British and Dutch trading ships, or been devised in China. Chinese literature mostly holds that it arrived by sea in the Ming dynasty, and the earliest record is in Li Kai's Hanzhong Ji of the Qing. Its name was originally written with the character for 'foreign' and was changed to the present one in 1910. It influenced the khim of Thailand and Cambodia, and the Korean yanggeum came from China in the eighteenth century. After the twentieth century the two-bridge small yangqin grew into three-, four- and five-bridge chromatic models and equal-tempered types, and from the 1950s steel alloy strings were adopted to increase volume.

The yangqin is a chordophone, H-S 314.122-4, belonging to the struck-dulcimer family; it has a flat trapezoidal wooden soundbox with several groups of metal strings, divided in pitch by bridges. The player holds a bamboo beater in each hand and strikes the strings alternately, and can also use the back of the beater, hook the strings with its tail or damp them by pressing. It has features of both percussion and strings; in the modern Chinese orchestra it is scored as a plucked instrument, and it is commonly used for solos, ensemble playing and accompaniment to huqin, dizi and other instruments, and it also appears in Cantonese music, Jiangnan sizhu, Chaozhou music, Sichuan yangqin, Shandong qinshu, Uyghur muqam and the Inner Mongolian errentai and similar settings.
揚琴琴身以木製成，呈扁平梯形音箱；發聲體為金屬弦，傳統用青銅弦，1950年代後改: The body of the yangqin is of wood, a flat trapezoidal soundbox; the sounding parts are metal strings, traditionally bronze, replaced since the 1950s by steel alloy, with copper-wound steel for the bass. The bridges are long wooden bars with raised string supports; at the sides are metal rollers or ball-shaped tuning pieces that raise the strings and adjust the pitch finely. The beaters are of bamboo, one end covered with rubber or another elastic material, and early instruments also used small wooden hammers. The source does not state the materials of the tuning screws, the tuning pins and the soundboard.
